# Confounding you cannot measure {#sec-frontdoor}

The trouble with observational data is rarely the data. It is that the thing
driving both the treatment and the outcome is often something nobody wrote down.

@fig-frontdoor states the problem precisely. Smoking raises tar deposits, and
tar deposits raise cancer risk; but something unmeasured — shared genetic
susceptibility — pushes on both smoking behaviour and cancer risk directly. The
dashed double-headed arrow is that unmeasured common cause. It is not a
variable in the model, because it is not a variable in the study.

![The front-door structure. The dashed bidirected edge denotes confounding that
was never measured.](figures/smoking-cancer-fig-frontdoor.svg){#fig-frontdoor}

What makes this structure worth drawing is that the effect of smoking on cancer
is still identifiable, despite the confounding, because the mediator is
measured and is not itself confounded with the outcome.

# When the instrument is the argument

@fig-iv shows the same problem attacked differently. Here nothing about local
demand is observed well enough to adjust for, so the design leans on a policy
change that moves labour cost without touching employment any other way.

![An instrumental-variable design.](figures/minimum-wage-fig-iv.svg){#fig-iv}

That last clause is the whole assumption, and it is the one the diagram makes
checkable: if the instrument had any arrow reaching employment that did not pass
through labour cost, the design would be invalid. The model is linted for
exactly that.
